u01_listen2_headache.texto: Do you get headaches from looking at computer screens? You're not alone. Many people look at computer screens for several hours a day. How can we avoid these terrible headaches? One reason we get headaches is because we look at the screen too closely for a long amount of time without any breaks. A good rule is the twenty-twenty-twenty rule. Every twenty minutes, take a twenty-second break and look at something twenty feet away. This will give your eyes time to relax. Another possible problem is that the room you're in is too bright. If there is too much light in the room, it can cause a problem for your eyes. If it's possible, try to turn down the lighting in the room. It will give your eyes a bit of a rest. Lastly, how you set up your desk can also cause problems. Is your computer screen too high or low? Do you have to look up or down a lot at your screen? It's best to put the screen at about ten centimeters below eye level and sit about forty centimeters away from the screen. You still need to take breaks, of course, but putting your screen in the right position can help while you're looking at it.

u02_listen2_plogging.texto: Many people ask me, what is plogging? To do plogging, simply go for a jog, but keep a trash bag on you. Every time you see trash, stop and pick it up, then continue jogging. Simple. The activity has become quite popular and, believe it or not, there are plogging competitions. The first world competition was in 2021 in Piedmont, Italy. It was more of a local contest, but in 2022, runners from over a dozen countries took part in that year's competition. They even held an opening ceremony before the race began, with runners displaying the flags from their countries. So how do you win a plogging race? After the race, judges check the distance that the runner ran, but there's more. The kind of trash they collected makes a difference in their score. If they collected a tissue paper, that's not worth much. But if they collected a car battery, that's quite a big score. Also, the altitude, or how high up the runner ran, matters in scoring. So a low, flat area gets a lower score than an area on a hill. Plogging is very good for the environment. In the 2023 competition in Genoa, Italy, ploggers collected an amazing 3,000 kilograms of trash. Wow!

u03_listen1_workinganimals.texto: The Tibetan Plateau is a very high area in southwestern China with mountains all around it, and it's not easy to get around. Luckily, the people of this area have help, the yak. The yak is an animal that looks like a cow, but with really big horns. Most of them are black, and believe it or not, there are more yaks, three hundred million, than Tibetan people, two hundred and sixty million. Yaks can carry up to two hundred kilograms of items fifteen kilometers per day. They are smart too, and they don't get scared easily. They are good at traveling across dangerous roads and know when to walk around a difficult place. On the other side of the world in Canada, Lester Courtney and his wife spend a lot of time with their horses, not for leisure, but for work. They are old-style tree loggers who cut trees in the traditional way. They also transport the trees traditionally with horses. Once the trees are down, Dan and Maddie pull them away. They are Lester's two horses. Lester has always used horses, and he thinks they are better than modern machines. For one thing, a horse isn't as heavy as modern machinery, so it doesn't damage the old forests. Lester also prefers horses because they aren't as noisy.

u04_listen2_groupwork.texto: Hi, I'm Jenna. I had a problem with a team member of my volleyball team. She was a good player, but when she made mistakes, she got very angry. My teammates and I wanted to find out why, so we invited her to a get-together over the weekend. While we were talking, we found out that her older sister was a champion volleyball player at university. She wanted to be just like her, but I explained that we can't compare ourselves to others. We have to find our own special skills. She seemed to enjoy playing a lot more, and now she's one of our best players. I'm Harry. My colleagues and I were training for a cross-country skiing event. There were eight of us, and I was a little worried because two of the team members didn't get on well. One day, they had a terrible fight. We let them argue for a while, and after they finished, I tried talking to them to find out what their problems were. Then I learned that they just didn't like each other. There was no way that they were going to get along. In the end, we said they should leave. If group members can't be pleasant with each other, they can't be in a group. My name is Aranya. When groups don't communicate well, they can be difficult to manage. I'll give you an example. I am part of a cycling team, and many of us have busy lives, so the times that we meet on weekends often change. One time, I came to one of our group meetings, and half of the people weren't there. I tried to find out why. It was because the organizer didn't tell us about a change in meeting time. We were quite unhappy. Two days later, I decided to talk to the organizer, and I offered to help communicate the times. I knew I would do a better job.

u06_listen1_countries.texto: Welcome to our show, Life Changes. We're here with Roberta, a designer who has lived in many countries. Roberta, how did your journey begin? I'm from Florida, and in my early twenties, I moved to Spain. I wanted to experience the place where my father grew up. And how was that? At first, I thought it was difficult. I knew Spanish, but not as well as I thought. And people live close to each other. There isn't much space for yards, and it was crowded. But I still had fun. And when did you move on? After some years, I met some Greek neighbors. They gave me the idea to live on a Greek island. So in my thirties, I moved to Naxos. The people there lived simple, comfortable lives. But you left, though. Why? I met a Polish tourist one summer, and we fell in love. So in my early forties, we moved to Poland and got married. This was hard because it's so much colder there. The language was difficult to learn, too. People didn't often speak English, unlike in Greece. And what's been the most interesting thing you've learned? People are nicer than you think. Locals were helpful when language was a problem. For anyone who wants to move abroad, I say go for it.

When the clay was wet, they pressed the stylus into it to make pictures or numbers. When the clay dried, they had a permanent record. It worked amazingly because we can still see today what they wrote down back then.

They changed the writing a bit, but we can see a connection with Sumerian. Now, this form of writing was very different from ours. If you look at it, you will think it's just pictures. Well, each picture shows an idea, which is how they communicated meaning. You can also see some signs that look like numbers. The pictures and numbers go together to make a record. People wrote down, for example, how much of a type of food they had or how many farm animals they had. We don't see writing from this period which tells us what these people thought about life. They just wrote down lists as far as we know. The way they wrote was with clay, a very soft material we get from the ground, and with a sort of pencil called a stylus. When the clay was wet, they pressed the stylus into it to make pictures or numbers. When the clay dried, they had a permanent record. It worked amazingly because we can still see today what they wrote down back then.

u12_listen2_greenland.texto: Greenland is special to me because it's where my dad's from. He and his parents left to live in Denmark forty years ago, so he could have a good education here. And in twenty twenty-two, after I finished my own studies, I decided to go there for a few months. I stayed with my cousins in Nuuk, Greenland's capital and largest city, with just twenty thousand people. I arrived in March. It was cold, about four degrees Celsius, but it wasn't dark all day. The sun rose at eight AM and set at six PM. It was fascinating to see the northern lights at night. The blues and the greens in the sky moved like ocean waves. My cousins took me to museums with local art and boats from historical times. We never left town, though. Did you know that Greenland has no highways? There are roads in towns, but not between them. You must travel by helicopter or ship. During summer, we went whale watching. Whales are important in Greenlandic culture. People have written stories about them for centuries. These animals are so big. They can weigh ninety thousand kilograms and be eighteen meters long. It was amazing to see them swimming in the ocean. I hope to return to Greenland someday. But in the meantime, my cousins will visit me. I can't wait to show them around.
